12. Graceful Degradation
------------------------

Each external system fails independently — one outage does not break a page.

| System | Failure mode |
| --- | --- |
| Contentful | Render page without editorial content; never block commerce data on CMS |
| Global-e | Surface explicit error; do not silently fall back to SFCC for international checkout |
| Didomi | Fail closed — no consent, no third-party scripts |
| Omneo (writes) / Emarsys | Queue and retry silently; never block the user flow |
| Omneo (reads) | **Load-bearing for My Account profile pages** — per DMU-004 only email + Omneo ID are migrated; all other customer profile data is sourced live from Omneo at login. Surface an explicit retry/error UI on profile pages if the round-trip fails; do not render stale or partial profile data. |
| Google Maps | Degrade to manual address entry; never hard-block checkout |
| AP21 (Retail Rewards) | On AP21 unavailability at the point of Rewards application, inform the customer and allow an alternative payment method |
| Narvar (EDD) | Suppress widget; do not show an error or block checkout |

### 12.1 Blast-Radius Containment

The failure modes above describe what the PWA does when a single integration is unavailable. This section covers how to limit the *spread* of an attack or outage — ensuring a degraded integration cannot consume shared resources and take down unrelated features.

#### Edge (outside the PWA — Infrastructure / SI Partner)

* **Web Application Firewalls + rate limiting** is the primary lever for volumetric attacks and credential-stuffing.
* **SFCC Business Manager** provides API-level rate limiting for SFCC endpoints, independent of the storefront edge.

#### SSR layer (inside the PWA)

`overrides/app/ssr.js` makes server-side `fetch` calls directly (token exchange, JWKS, SF Payments metadata). Node's native `fetch` is backed by `undici` internally. Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. This prevents a slow or flooded integration (e.g. checkout APIs) from exhausting connections for unrelated origins (e.g. Contentful, JWKS).

> **Implementation note:** the per-call `dispatcher` option is safer than the `setGlobalDispatcher` in a managed environment (MRT) since it does not touch the global dispatcher that Salesforce internal libraries may rely on. The `commerce-sdk-react` hooks manage their own HTTP client server-side (Commerce SDK) and are not affected in either approach.

The connection pool split is an engineering decision — the right pool boundaries and sizes depend on observed traffic patterns and the integration map in §7. Planned pools (connection caps should be validated later — see §9.3):

| Pool | Origin | Calls | Cap | `connectTimeout` | `bodyTimeout` | Reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sfcc-scapi` | `<https://{shortCode}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com`> | SLAS JWKS (token validation for passwordless login, reset password) | 5 | 5 s | 8 s | `jose` caches the JWK set for its rotation period; actual network calls are rare. Isolated so a JWKS fetch is never starved by higher-volume pools. |
| `sfcc-payments` | `config.app.sfPayments.metadataUrl` host (a `*.demandware.net` or SCAPI hostname — waiting confirmation from Mani) | Payment method metadata on every checkout page SSR | 10 | 5 s | 8 s | Called on every checkout page load; moderate frequency. Separate from `sfcc-scapi` because a checkout traffic spike must not consume SLAS connections. |
| `mulesoft` | `MULESOFT_BASE_URL` | Order history, order details, boutique / BOPIS stock check, GiveX balance check | 20 | 5 s | 10 s | Highest user-facing concurrency (My Account + PDP). GiveX balance calls carry payment credentials in the POST body — a slow MuleSoft response must not hold connections open and starve other pools. Highest cap reflects the broadest call surface. |
| `marketing-cloud-auth` | `<https://{subdomain}.auth.marketingcloudapis.com`> | Marketing Cloud client-credentials token exchange | 5 | 5 s | 15 s | User-triggered, infrequent; token cached at module scope for 15 min. Isolated so an MC outage cannot consume SFCC or MuleSoft connections. |
| `marketing-cloud-rest` | `<https://{subdomain}.rest.marketingcloudapis.com`> | Magic-link email send (passwordless login, reset password) | 5 | 5 s | 15 s | Same trigger as above; higher body timeout because email delivery APIs can respond slowly under load. |
| `google-places` | `<https://places.googleapis.com`> (Places API — New) | Address autocomplete at checkout (CFD-023, CFD-030, CFD-059) | 5 | 3 s | 5 s | Non-critical-path; graceful fallback to manual entry. Short timeouts ensure a Places API slowdown releases connections quickly. |
| `booxi` | Booxi base URL (TBD) | Boutique appointment read in My Account (CRM-165–167) | 5 | 3 s | 5 s | My Account only; non-critical-path within that page. |

**Contentful:** The Contentful SDK (`contentful` v11) does not expose a `dispatcher` hook on its internal fetch calls, so connection isolation for Contentful is not achievable through this pattern. Primary mitigation is the graceful degradation rule in §12 (Render page without editorial content).

13. Testing Strategy
--------------------

Three layers, no duplicated coverage — the cheapest layer that proves a behaviour wins.

| Layer | Tool | Covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | Vitest | Pure logic, data mapping, transforms, isolated hooks |
| Component interaction | Storybook `play` | Single-component user interactions |
| E2E | Playwright | Full journeys, multi-region, integration boundaries |

### 13.1 What is tested

Failure paths that would be non-obvious or costly to debug: Contentful → component data mapping, locale / currency transforms, Global-e pricing / tax branching, checkout ownership, consent gating, cart mutations, optimistic-update rollback. Framework behaviour and pure visual rendering are not tested at this layer.

### 13.2 E2E gherkin-first workflow

Every Playwright spec starts as a Gherkin `.feature` file that Lead QA validates in plain English before any code is written. This prevents technically correct tests of the wrong behaviour.

### 13.3 Multi-region fixtures

E2E specs are parameterised by `SITE_ID` from day one — every journey runs across all 8 storefronts and 11 active locales, with site-specific `baseUrl`, currency, checkout owner, tax model, and consent default supplied by a fixture rather than hardcoded. (Because a test hardcoded to one region cannot be cheaply expanded later)

### 13.4 Selector priority

Tests select elements the way users and assistive tech perceive them: accessible selectors (role + name, label, visible text) first, semantic HTML attributes second (`alt`, `title`), `data-testid` only when nothing semantic applies. Tag/class/DOM-position selectors are not used. This doubles as a continuous accessibility check.

Stage is the **contractual performance-test environment** referenced in §9.3 — it mirrors production infrastructure (same MRT bundle class, CDN/edge configuration, SFCC realm tier).

### 14.2 Branch model

GitFlow with explicit back-merges to keep `develop` aligned with production.

| Branch | Branched from | Merges to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `feature/*` | `develop` | `develop` |
| `fix/*` | `develop` | `develop` |
| `release/*` | `develop` | `main` **and** `develop` |
| `fix/release-{version}-*` | the `release/*` branch | the `release/*` branch (forward-merged to `develop` via the release back-merge) |
| `hotfix/*` | `main` | `main` **and** `develop` |
| `develop`, `main` | — | protected; PR-only |

Release branches are supervised — code logic fixes go on a `fix/release-{version}-*` sub-branch rather than directly on the release branch. Releases and hotfixes always back-merge to `develop` so production fixes flow forward automatically.

### 14.3 CI workflows

**QA workflow (**`qa.yml`) — runs on every PR to `develop` and `release/**`. Code-correctness checks with no environment dependency:

* Unit tests (Vitest)
* Storybook interaction tests (`play` functions) and component-level accessibility checks via `@storybook/addon-a11y` (`storybook test --ci`)

**SIT gate (**`digital-sit.yml`) — runs on push/PR to `release/**`; on merge to `develop` it also deploys to the **Dev** environment (tier 2 in §14.1). Environment-dependent checks:

* Playwright `p0` priority specs
* Bundle-size check against the ceilings in §9
* Contract tests against the MuleSoft OpenAPI specification
* Lighthouse CI thresholds (Performance ≥ 0.80, Accessibility ≥ 0.90, Best Practices ≥ 0.90)
* Trend gate against the LHCI history server

### 14.4 Deployment

Deployment is via Salesforce Managed Runtime. Each tier maps to its own MRT target:

* **Dev** — deployed on merge to `develop`, gated on a clean SIT gate (§14.3)
* **SIT** — deployed on the NewStore release cadence, isolated from the Digital release path (failures do not block `release/**`)
* **Stage** — deployed on a booked 2-week window for full end-to-end testing with live third parties
* **UAT** — deployed for business acceptance; promotion requires Business sign-off
* **Prod** — release-manager-gated; AU canary first, then flag-flip to remaining regions

Production deploys are gated on a clean SIT gate run plus stakeholder approval through Stage and UAT.

MRT deployment targets map one-to-one to the topology: `dev | sit | stage | uat | production`."

Verified — Jhoan's PWA TSD claim checks out. Here's the sufficiency verdict for each.

## Reply #2 (Centralized Filtering Logic) — Sufficient ✅

This is a strong answer. It does exactly what Tim's question ("what do we mean by this") needed:
- States concretely what "centralized" means (all ID-matching lives in the SSR layer, no component does its own filtering)
- Gives a real example failure mode (a missing null-ID check)
- Explains the actual blast radius (every page of that type breaks at once, with no secondary check to catch it, since the component trusts whatever it's handed and never validates)
- Points to §5.3's exact pseudocode for the full logic

I checked the "no secondary check to catch it" claim against our own component contract (§5.3: the component "holds no SFCC ID comparison logic... renders all entries it receives") and it's accurate. No gaps here.

## Reply #1 (SSR Cache Keys) — Partially sufficient, one real weak spot

Her reply has two parts, and they're not equally strong:

**"This is verified in 4.3 Trade-offs Accepted"** — this is circular, not verification. §4.3 just restates the *same claim* in slightly different words ("Every SSR cache key for an ID-scoped page must include the SFCC ID; omitting it leaks editorial content across category or product pages"). Pointing at your own document repeating itself isn't evidence the claim is true, it's just evidence the claim appears twice. If Tim (or anyone rigorous) pushes on this, "it's verified elsewhere in the same doc" won't hold up.

**"The PWA TSD also confirms full SSR for PDP and PLP pages"** — this part I checked directly, and it's accurate. PWA TSD 256835585 states verbatim: *"PDP, PLP, content pages, homepages, boutique pages | Full SSR, markup and data rendered on the server | Indexable, SEO- and LCP-critical."* So this half is real, genuine, external verification, not circular.

**But it only half-closes the loop.** "PDP/PLP are Full SSR" establishes that these pages *are* server-rendered and cached, it doesn't, on its own, prove that the cache key specifically needs to vary by SFCC ID. That's a logical step she implies but doesn't spell out. And there was a stronger piece of evidence available that she didn't use: `01-sfcc.md:93` already documents the existing SFCC edge cache as **"cache keys include site, locale, currency, and customer group."** That's the closest thing to a smoking gun, an already-proven precedent of exactly this principle (vary the cache key by every dimension that changes the output) already working in production today. Citing that would have made the answer airtight instead of implied.

## Bottom line

Reply #2: solid, leave as is. Reply #1: directionally correct and probably good enough to satisfy Tim as written, but has a genuine logical weak point (the circular §4.3 citation) and misses the strongest available evidence. Want me to draft a tightened version of reply #1 that drops the circular citation and adds the `01-sfcc.md:93` precedent?

we've already identified the case for both: "Good, found something concrete to ground this in, not just "common sense."

Where these cons come from, and what they mean
Con #1: "SSR cache keys must include the SFCC ID or cached content leaks across pages."

ELI5: Picture two shoppers, one browsing "Dresses," one browsing "Shirts." Both category pages might show a Contentful-authored banner. If we cache the server-rendered response to save work, and that cache doesn't know "this saved copy is for Dresses, that one is for Shirts," it can accidentally hand the Dresses banner to the Shirts page, or vice versa. The fix is: bake the category/product ID into the cache's storage key, so a Dresses-page cache entry and a Shirts-page cache entry are never confused for each other.

Where it's from: this isn't a fact someone looked up, it's a basic, well-known caching rule ("the cache key must include everything that changes what's inside the response"), applied to this specific pattern. But it's not just abstract theory either, I checked, and this exact principle is already proven and already in use today: 01-sfcc.md:93 documents the existing SFCC edge cache: "cache keys include site, locale, currency, and customer group." Option A's con is just saying: add one more thing to that same list, the SFCC category/product ID. It's not a new risky idea, it's the same pattern the system already relies on, extended by one dimension.

Con #2: "Filtering logic is centralised in the MRT SSR layer, which must be correct."

ELI5: Option A puts ALL the "does this content belong on this page?" decision-making in one shared place (the SSR layer), instead of scattering it across every individual component. Good: one place to get it right, consistent everywhere. Bad: if that one shared place has a bug, every content type using this pattern breaks at the same time, not just one isolated component.

Where it's from: also a basic software truism, centralizing logic always trades "consistency" for "single point of failure." It's true by definition, not something SFCC-specific. Tim's actual complaint wasn't "prove this," it was "what do we mean by this," the sentence is just too vague as written, it doesn't say what breaking looks like.

Confirmation status, and what's needed
Neither con is, or can be, empirically tested right now. Both describe a mechanism (the SSR-first fetch) that doesn't exist in code yet, there's nothing to run and check. Both are "this will be true once built, if built correctly" statements, not "this is true today" statements. That's the honest answer to Tim's "verified or a Claude assumption" question, it's neither, it's a design consequence.

Con #1: Backed by real precedent (01-sfcc.md:93), not invented. What's needed: reword to say plainly it's a design requirement (not a tested fact, since the mechanism isn't built), and cite the existing SFCC cache-key precedent so it reads as "consistent with how this system already works" rather than a bare assertion. Nobody outside us needs to weigh in, this is a documentation-clarity fix we can do ourselves.
Con #2: True by definition, just too vague. What's needed: reword to name the actual failure mode (a bug in the shared filter breaks every ID-targeted content type at once, not just one), so the sentence answers "what do we mean" instead of leaving it open.
Want me to draft the exact replacement text for both, like we did for the earlier comments?"

Let me think through this precisely, since "remove and reply" has different consequences for each of the 3 items, they're not actually uniform.

## The 3 items aren't the same kind of thing

**Item 1 (§2.2, Sprint-2 assumption row)** is just a *warning*, it contains no specifics of its own, it only flags that specifics exist elsewhere (Appendix C). **Removing it is actually safe**, I checked, and §7 already carries near-identical wording: *"Sprint-2 content-type field sets are inferred, not confirmed... Authoring walkthrough with Emma and Dani before locking fields; keep provisional."* So this row is redundant with §7 already, deleting it loses nothing, it's deduplication, not information loss.

**Item 2 (§5.2, the `sfccCategoryId`/`sfccProductId` field row)** actually contains real specifics, but the *same* field-level detail (types, localization, descriptions, the schema-as-code example) is fully documented in §5.3. So removing this row from §5.2 doesn't remove the specifics from the TSD, it just removes one of two places they're stated. The underlying content survives.

**Item 3 (§5.2, "one component per content type" row)** is already abstract, it doesn't name any specific content type or field. There's barely any volatile content in it to begin with. Removing it costs almost nothing either way.

## The real implication: this closes the comments, but doesn't solve what Tim actually asked for

Tim's stated problem was: *"it can drift quickly and we need to update multiple pages."* His proposed fix was a new artefact (component requirement pages) to be the single place this content lives. Deleting these 3 rows doesn't create that single source of truth, it just reduces how many copies of the content exist inside *this one document*. The specifics still live in Appendix C, §5.3, and eventually Jira tickets, none of which get consolidated by this action. So: **we'd be resolving the 3 inline comment threads, but not the underlying multi-page-drift problem he described.** If he comes back later expecting an actual replacement page, we'd be redoing this.

## A completeness risk in §5.2 specifically

The template's own rule for §5 is that it "must be specific enough for a developer who was not in any meeting to build from." If rows 2 and 3 both come out, §5.2's Component/API Changes table drops from 6 rows to 4, and it stops mentioning two of the most load-bearing build tasks: adding the SFCC-ID fields to content types, and building one component per content type. A developer reading only §5.2 would miss both. Since the actual field detail survives in §5.3, this is recoverable, but §5.2 alone would no longer stand on its own as a complete build checklist, which is a real, if narrow, template-conformance regression.

## What the reply should honestly say, if we go this route

"We took them out" is accurate for all three, but "and noted it" needs to mean different things per item, or the reply overstates what happened:
- Item 1: fair to say it's removed *because* it duplicates §7, point to that row.
- Item 2: honest framing is "removed from 5.2; the field definitions still live in 5.3 and Appendix C until we agree on where they permanently belong", not "resolved."
- Item 3: fair to say simply removed, since it's near-empty of specifics.

## Bottom line

This is a legitimate, low-effort way to close out the 3 inline comment threads today, and item 1 is genuinely a clean win with zero downside. Items 2 and 3 are safe from a content-loss standpoint too, since nothing actually disappears from the TSD as a whole. But it trades Tim's actual proposal (a durable single source of truth) for a surface fix (fewer duplicate copies on one page), and it risks him reading "removed" as "solved" when the multi-page drift problem he named is still open. Worth deciding whether that trade is acceptable, or whether the reply should explicitly flag that the structural question (component requirement pages) is still unresolved and pending his/Natasha's/Isabel's input, separate from these 3 closures.

content.text:
Here's the full picture of this one, pulling together everything we've established across the session.

## What the comments actually say

Both are anchored in **§5.5, "Authoring-path rule - Studio Experiences versus coded content-type components"**:

- **#13** (on the rule itself): *"I'm not sure we need to separate these and the components we build will most of the time being used in an experience builder."*
- **#14** (on the Heuristic bullet): *"Authors will place elements on a page."*

Together they're one challenge: Tim doubts the whole premise of a two-path split, and specifically rejects the criterion we used to draw the line ("does the author decide placement?"), on the grounds that author-placement is the norm, not a distinguishing edge case.

## Why this isn't a quick wording fix

Unlike the connector-app correction or the locale question, Tim didn't hand us a fact to correct against, he raised an opinion/objection with no stated resolution. And the rule he's pushing back on wasn't arbitrary, we established it this session by checking the actual codebase: `experiences/` uses `defineComponents` + `/:slug` for whole author-composed pages (Z.immerse, campaign pages), `overrides/app/components/contentful/` is hand-built for fixed template slots (homepage, footer, nav, etc.). Changing it without more than an opinion behind it would mean reversing a validated technical finding on the strength of "I'm not sure," which isn't enough on its own.

## What the investigation actually found

This is the part that changes things. Digging through Jira, Confluence, and the codebase turned up real, concrete evidence, not just Tim's opinion:

- **SFCC-51 (Promotional Announcement Banner), already-accepted AC:** *"the promotional banner is placed on a PDP or PLP via Contentful Studio, when it is configured with one or more SFCC Category IDs and/or Product IDs..."* Our TSD's §5.5 explicitly lists "announcement banner" as an example of a **coded** component. That's directly contradicted by Tim's own prior, already-accepted decision on this exact ticket. So this isn't just his opinion in the TSD comment, it's backed by a real precedent we got wrong in our own example list.
- **An unmerged draft dev guide** (`humanContentfulGuide.md`, PR #38, not signed off) independently says the **homepage** is "planned to be an Experience", which also contradicts our §5.5 classification of homepage modules as coded. But it disagrees with SFCC-51 on the banner specifically, calling it a regular coded entry. So two sources both push toward "more things become Studio Experience than our rule assumes," but they don't agree on which things.
- **HPC-010** ("reusable page builder templates across page types") is a weak, ambiguous hint, it never names Contentful, Studio, or Experience Builder, so it doesn't resolve anything on its own.
- Footer, nav, PLP inserts, and PDP tabs have **zero evidence** either way in Jira or Confluence.

Net effect: the banner misclassification is proven. The broader claim ("most of the time") is corroborated in spirit by two independent sources, but not settled for anything beyond the banner.

## What accepting this fully would ripple into

If Tim's position is taken at face value, it's not a §5.5-only fix:

- **§3/§4 (Option A itself)** describes SFCC-ID targeting as a coded-component + SSR-filter mechanism. SFCC-51's actual accepted design has the author configuring category/product targeting *inside a Studio placement*, a different mechanism entirely. Option A would need a second documented sub-pattern, not just a relabel.
- **§5.2** rows would shift emphasis toward the `experiences/` path as the default location for new work.
- **§7** would need a new risk: placing a Studio-authored, ID-targeted component into an existing PWA-Kit page (PDP/PLP) isn't a mechanism that exists in the codebase today, today's `experiences/` pattern only composes whole pages at a slug, it doesn't inject into an existing template. That new risk directly overlaps with the two already-uncarded spikes in §7 (PLP grid-injection pagination, PDP accordion mixed-content), since all three are really the same underlying question: how does external content get safely injected into an SFCC-rendered commerce page.
- **§8, Appendix A, Appendix C** would all need matching adjustments (ownership boundary, the banner's/PLP-insert's/PDP-accordion's stated mechanism).

## Current status: unresolved, still needs Tim's answer

Nothing here can be closed with a document edit alone. What's genuinely proven is narrow: the banner example is wrong and should move. What's still open is the scope, does "most of the time" mean footer, nav, homepage modules, PLP inserts, and PDP tabs too, or just the banner? Neither Jira nor Confluence answers that, and the two sources we found don't agree with each other on it either.

## How this actually gets resolved

One direct question to Tim, in the sync: **beyond the announcement banner (already confirmed via SFCC-51), which other components does he mean by "most of the time", specifically footer, nav, homepage modules, PLP inserts, and PDP tabs?** And a second, technical follow-up worth surfacing alongside it: **does he expect a mechanism for placing a Studio-authored component inside an existing PDP/PLP page, since that doesn't exist in the codebase yet, and if so, is that the same problem as the two already-uncarded PLP-pagination and PDP-accordion spikes, or a separate one?**

Once we have that answer, the fix becomes concrete: correct the banner example immediately (that part needs no further alignment, it's already proven), and scope the rest of §5.5's rewrite, plus the §3/§4/§7 ripple, to whatever Tim actually confirms.

content.text:
Good call to isolate it, because #14 is genuinely coupled to #13 in one direction but not the other, worth being precise about that before proposing anything.

## The dependency, stated honestly

- **If #13 resolves to "drop the two-path split entirely"** (everything becomes Studio Experience), #14 becomes moot. There's no heuristic needed if there's only one path, the whole bullet just gets deleted along with the rest of the rule. Nothing to fix.
- **If #13 resolves to "keep some version of the split"** (even a narrower one than today), #14 needs an actual answer: the current criterion ("does the author decide placement?") doesn't hold, per Tim, so it has to be replaced with something else.

So #14 can't be fully closed without knowing how #13 lands. But there's a real, useful piece of work we can do *now*, independent of Tim's answer: figure out what the replacement criterion should be, so it's ready the moment #13 is settled, rather than waiting to start thinking about it then.

## A candidate replacement criterion, grounded in evidence we already have

Going back to SFCC-51: what actually made the banner Studio-placed wasn't "an author touches it", authors touch almost everything, including footer copy and nav links. It's that the banner's **placement itself is a moving target**: it can live on Home, PDP, PLP, or "Global across all but Z.immerse," and which page it's on is a merchandising decision that can change. Compare that to footer, nav, or size guide: those are always in the exact same structural slot, on every relevant page, forever. Authors edit their *content* (copy, links), never their *position*.

That suggests the actual discriminator isn't "does an author touch this", it's:

> **Does this content's placement itself vary or change over time (a campaign/merchandising decision, potentially moving between pages)? → Studio Experience.**
> **Is this a structurally fixed piece of UI that always renders in the same slot, where only the field values (not the position) are editable? → Coded component.**

This has a real advantage: it correctly explains why the banner reclassifies (its placement moves) while leaving footer, nav, and size guide exactly where they already are (their placement never moves), it doesn't require blowing up the whole classification, just fixing the one thing SFCC-51 actually proved was wrong.

**To be clear about what this is:** this is my proposed synthesis from the evidence, not something Tim has confirmed. It's a candidate answer to have ready, not a decision. Whether it's the right replacement criterion, and whether the split survives #13 at all, both still need Tim's sign-off in the sync.

## What's actually needed for #14, concretely

1. Nothing to write into the doc yet, it still depends on #13's outcome.
2. But we now have a ready answer to propose if #13 keeps some split: swap "who decides placement" for "does placement itself change over time."
3. If #13 kills the split entirely, #14 just gets deleted, no replacement needed.

For the broader BA/Tester process this plugs into (story intake → AC → Zephyr test cases → this layer → BrowserStack → defect triage), see [AI-Assisted QA — Overview & Methodology](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/277544962) and Guides 1–3.

Scope
-----

This guide covers the **E2E layer** only. It is additive to — not a replacement for — the unit and component-interaction layers:

| Layer | Tooling | Lives in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit (pure logic) | Vitest | `*.test.ts` alongside the source |
| Component interaction | Storybook `play` functions | `*.stories.tsx` alongside the component |

Model
-----

Human-in-the-lead. Claude Code generates tests — a Lead QA validates them.

**Rule:** never treat test generation as complete until the Lead QA has approved the `.feature` file.

DefaultnoneDeveloper writes story →

Playwright .spec.ts is generated →
Test is committed

│ │ ├── basePage.ts

This is a slim overrides project, not a fork of the upstream PWA Kit monorepo — there is no `e2e/tests/desktop/` or `e2e/tests/mobile/` Salesforce scaffold to preserve.

Writing a feature file
----------------------

* One `.feature` file per Jira story
* File name: `{JIRA-KEY}_{short-description}.feature`
* Every file needs: Jira tag (`@SFCC-NNN`), area tag (`@checkout` etc.), and `@p0` if it's a critical path
* At least one happy path and one failure/edge scenario
* Plain English only — no selectors, no code, no technical detail

Generating tests with /qa-generate
----------------------------------

In a Claude Code session: `/qa-generate`. The skill asks for Jira story details, drafts the `.feature` file, pauses for Lead QA validation, then generates the Playwright spec and any required Page Object additions.

Only run this on a feature branch. Never on `develop` or `main`.

Page Object Model — selector priority
-------------------------------------

Enforced in code review:

1. **Accessible selectors** — role + accessible name, label, visible text (`getByRole`, `getByLabelText`, `getByText`). First choice.
2. **Semantic HTML attributes** — `getByAltText`, `getByTitle`, `getByPlaceholderText`.
3. **`data-testid`** — last resort only, for elements with no semantic meaning.

Selectors live in `e2e/support/pages/` only. Never write selectors directly in test files.

--------------------------

Zimmermann serves 6 regions (AU, US, UK, EU, ME, HK) across **7 SFCC sites** (AU, UK, US, EU domestic, EU international, HK, ME — US confirmed as a single site, REG-005). All test data must be region-aware from day one — keyed by `SITE_ID` rather than retrofitted.

Read Jesse's conventions page in full and checked the actual E2E folder. This surfaces a real, useful gap, and one incidental discrepancy worth flagging separately.

## What Jesse's guide establishes (the rules any Contentful E2E work has to follow)

- Architecture: Gherkin `.feature` files (one per Jira story) → generated Playwright `.spec.ts`, via `/qa-generate`, always validated by Lead QA before being generated/committed.
- **"Never hardcode test data in test files, always use `e2e/fixtures/`."** Fixtures today: `site.js` (regional config), `customers.js`, `products.js`, `orders.js`. Tests are environment-aware via `SITE_ID`.
- Deterministic test data is pinned via dedicated secrets: `E2E_STANDARD_PRODUCT_SKU`, `E2E_VARIANT_PRODUCT_SKU`, `E2E_OOS_PRODUCT_SKU`, `E2E_SALE_PRODUCT_SKU`, `E2E_FIXTURE_ORDER_NUMBER`. That's the team's existing pattern for "make an E2E assertion deterministic against a live system": pin a known, dedicated record by ID, don't assert against arbitrary real data.
- Tests run primarily against **SIT** (`npm run test:sit` is what gates Digital SIT).

## What actually exists for Contentful today: nothing

`e2e/` has exactly one feature/test in the whole repo (`SMOKE-homepage-load`), and zero Contentful-related fixtures, page objects, or conventions. This isn't a gap in our TSD alone, it's genuinely greenfield in the codebase. So Jesse's ask isn't "clarify a detail", it's "there's no pattern for this yet, let's define one."

## The actual discussion to have with Jesse

The core question is exactly the one Jesse named: **how does a Playwright test know what Contentful content to expect on a given page, when that content is CMS-managed and can change?** Framed against his own conventions, the natural answer follows the same shape as the SKU-secret pattern already in use:

- A dedicated, **known E2E test entry** seeded in the Contentful `sit` environment (e.g., a test banner or PLP insert with a fixed `sfccCategoryId`), referenced by ID via a secret or fixture, the same way `E2E_STANDARD_PRODUCT_SKU` pins a known product. Asserting against arbitrary real editorial content would be non-deterministic, editors could change or unpublish it between test runs.
- That implies a **new fixture file** analogous to `products.js`, something like `e2e/fixtures/content.js`, holding the known Contentful entry IDs/scoping values per region/environment, which doesn't exist yet and isn't proposed anywhere.
- Environment targeting matters too: Contentful has its own environment tiers (dev/test/sit/staging/uat/production per our §5.5), so whichever environment E2E runs against needs its own seeded test entries, kept in sync the same way `sit`-specific SFCC fixtures are today.

## Why this can't be fully answered yet, and what it depends on

This ties directly into open items already in our §7: you can't write a deterministic Playwright assertion for "the PLP grid insert doesn't break pagination" before that mechanism itself is even spiked (the uncarded PLP-pagination item), and the same is true for the PDP accordion mixed-content spike and SFCC-238's reference-resolution work. Those three unresolved items effectively gate what QA can concretely test, worth naming explicitly to Jesse so it's clear this isn't being deprioritized, it's sequenced behind design decisions that haven't landed yet.

## One incidental finding, unrelated to the main ask

Jesse's own conventions page states: *"Zimmermann serves 6 regions... across 7 SFCC sites... US confirmed as a single site, REG-005."* That directly conflicts with what we verified this session, US-International is planned as a **separate** site (`ZimmermannUSIntl`), not merged into a single US site. Also, the page's "Open item" note says `config/sites.js` is "still the OOTB Salesforce default", which is stale, the generate+overlay pattern is already built. Worth a quick heads-up to Jesse or whoever owns that page, separate from the testing-coverage discussion itself.

## What this call is actually about (one sentence)

content.text:
Here's a Q&A prep sheet, grouped by the kind of question a QA lead would actually ask, with the simple answer ready to go.

## "What are we even testing?"

**Q: What's the actual behavior here?**
A: That a piece of Contentful content, like a banner, only shows up on the page it's supposed to (a specific category, say), and doesn't show up anywhere else. If the editor didn't restrict it, it shows everywhere. That's the whole thing at its core.

**Q: Is this testing Contentful, or SFCC, or both?**
A: Both, it's really testing the *connection* between them. The test needs to check two things: did the Contentful entry get the right SFCC ID configured, and did our code correctly show or hide it based on which page you're actually on. So it's genuinely end to end, not one side or the other.

## "Why is this different from a normal test?"

**Q: Why can't we just test this like any other component?**
A: Because the content itself lives in a separate system (Contentful) that editors change independently of our code. A normal component test uses fake data we fully control. Here, we need a stable, known piece of test content to point at, not whatever's "really live" that day, since that could change or disappear on us mid-test.

## "Who owns the test data?"

**Q: Who creates and maintains this test content in Contentful?**
A: Genuinely open right now, nobody owns it yet. For products, someone already keeps the test SKUs consistent. For Contentful, that'll probably land with either the content team or whoever runs the CI service account, still needs deciding.

**Q: What if an editor accidentally changes or deletes the test entry?**
A: That's exactly why we want *dedicated* test entries, not real editorial content, ideally locked down the same way we already restrict who can edit content types in certain environments, so regular editors can't touch them by accident.

## "When and where does this actually happen?"

**Q: When can we actually write these tests?**
A: Not yet. Three things have to land first: the actual server-side rendering code (doesn't exist yet, still client-side today), whether inserting content into a product grid breaks pagination (open question), and how a mixed Contentful-and-SFCC accordion works on the product page (also undecided). Testing follows the build, not the other way round.

**Q: Which environment do these tests run against?**
A: Following the existing pattern, product tests hit SIT, so Contentful tests probably should too. Needs confirming, not assuming.

**Q: Do we need this across all 8 storefronts?**
A: Eventually, probably, since content and locale do vary. But given how much isn't built yet, better to prove the pattern on one representative storefront first, then expand, rather than trying to cover everything on day one.

## "How does this fit what we already do?"

**Q: Does this go through the same Zephyr → feature file → Playwright pipeline?**
A: Yes, nothing new there. Once the actual Jira stories for these components get built, same pipeline as everything else. The only genuinely new thing is deciding, once, how tests point at known Contentful content, so every team building a Contentful-driven story doesn't invent their own way.

**Q: Do the Jira stories already have AC for this scoping behavior?**
A: Honestly, not yet, that lives in the TSD design right now. Worth flagging that it needs to be added to each story's AC when it's actually picked up, so it shows up in the generated `.feature` files.

**Q: Could this slow down or interfere with existing product tests?**
A: Shouldn't, if scoped properly, it'd be its own fixture file and its own feature files, same pattern as products/customers/orders, just a new lane, not touching the existing ones.

## "Why loop me in now, if the tests are downstream?"

**Q: If the actual tests belong to later build stories, why is this call happening now?**

You now have a real, current example instead of a hypothetical: these three tickets already assume "wait for real content," while the established E2E convention says "use fixed, known fixtures." Tax calculation in the Zimmermann SFCC platform is handled by **Avalara AvaTax**. SFCC is the orchestration layer — it initiates tax estimate requests during checkout and commits the final tax record when an order is placed. Tax data originates in **AP21** (product TaxCodes and HS codes), flows through SFCC, and is consumed downstream by **NewStore** for fulfilment and returns.

There are two distinct tax flows:

| Flow | Direction | Trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Forward: Estimate & Commit | SFCC → Avalara | Customer adds to cart / places order |
| Reverse: Tax Reversal | NewStore → Avalara (via ReturnInvoice) | Customer initiates return via Narvar |

---

2. Systems Involved
-------------------

| System | Role |
| --- | --- |
| AP21 | System of record for product TaxCodes and HS (Harmonised System) duty codes |
| SFCC | Orchestrates tax estimate (SalesOrder) and commit (SalesInvoice) calls to Avalara |
| Avalara AvaTax | Tax calculation engine — address validation, jurisdiction lookup, rate calculation, filing |
| NewStore | Fulfils orders; initiates tax reversal (ReturnInvoice) for customer returns |
| Narvar | Customer-facing return portal; triggers webhook to NewStore on return initiation |

---

3. Flow 1: Forward Order & Fulfilment
-------------------------------------

true100%Tax1804px

### 3.1 Product Data Setup — AP21 (async, separate from order flow)

AP21 is the system of record for product tax attributes. This data is synced to SFCC asynchronously via MuleSoft as a background process — it is **not** part of the per-transaction order sequence.

| AP21 Attribute | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Tax Category | Groups products by taxability type |
| TaxCode | Avalara-compatible code used for rate determination |
| HS Code | Harmonised System tariff code for cross-border duty calculation |

### 3.2 Tax Estimate (Cart → Checkout)

1. Customer adds items to cart. SFCC creates a basket with product TaxCode and HS code attached.
2. SFCC sends a **SalesOrder** (tax estimate request) to Avalara including TaxCode and HS codes per line item.
3. Avalara validates the shipping address.
4. Avalara identifies applicable tax jurisdictions based on the shipping address.
5. Avalara applies taxability rules per TaxCode.
6. Avalara returns the calculated tax estimate to SFCC.
7. SFCC displays the estimated tax to the customer at checkout.

### 3.3 Tax Commit (Order Placement)

1. Customer confirms and places the order.
2. SFCC sends a **SalesInvoice** to Avalara — this commits the tax transaction.
3. Avalara records the transaction and files tax returns per applicable jurisdiction.
4. Avalara returns commit confirmation to SFCC.

### 3.4 Fulfilment (SFCC → NewStore)

1. SFCC dispatches the committed order and tax details to NewStore.
2. NewStore receives the order, routes to the appropriate fulfilment location, picks, packs, and ships.
3. NewStore sends shipment confirmation and tracking back to SFCC.
4. SFCC updates the order status and notifies the customer.

---

4. Flow 2: Return & Tax Reversal
--------------------------------

true100%Reversal1084px

### 4.1 Return Initiation (Narvar)

1. Customer initiates a return via the Narvar return portal.
2. Narvar issues an RMA and carrier label to the customer.
3. Narvar fires a webhook to NewStore notifying of the return event.

### 4.2 Return Processing & Tax Reversal (NewStore → Avalara)

1. NewStore receives the returned item at the fulfilment location.
2. Item is inspected and restocked.
3. NewStore sends a **ReturnInvoice** to Avalara — this initiates the tax reversal.
4. Avalara creates a credit memo reversing the original tax amount.
5. Avalara adjusts the filed tax returns per applicable jurisdiction.
6. Avalara confirms the reversal to NewStore.
7. NewStore issues the refund and notifies the customer.

---

content.text:
This turned into a genuinely important finding, there's actually no true "approved TSD under the current template" to compare against, and that itself matters. Here's the full three-way picture.

## Finding #1: no approved precedent exists under the current 8-section template

I checked the whole "TSD: X — Y" family (Tax, Catalogue Sync, Product Attributes, Inventory, Price, Product, Orders), all of them use a completely different, older, free-form structure ("1. Overview," "2. Systems Involved," flow diagrams, "Key Concepts"), none have a Document Information table, a Decision Record, a Sign-off table, or anything called "Testing & Validation." Same for PWA TSD and Product TSD, which we've read extensively this session. **None of these use the current template at all.** So there's no genuine like-for-like precedent of "an approved TSD, same template, populated §6" to hold ours up against, ours may be one of the first real attempts to fill this section out under this exact structure.

## Finding #2: the closest real precedent is the PWA TSD's Testing Strategy, and it goes much deeper than the template's bare minimum

| Source | What it actually says |
|---|---|
| **Template's own guidance** | "Describe how you will confirm the solution works... map directly to Section 1.4... at minimum: unit test coverage, one P0 Playwright scenario, and any integration test requirements." Table shape only, placeholders like "[Component or hook under test]", no depth implied beyond the shape itself. |
| **Our SFCC-249 draft (§6)** | A short justification ("this spike produces findings and a design, not a testable build") + a 4-row table naming *what* future tests should check (e.g. "Filter selects matching + null-ID entries only") + one regression-risk paragraph. Stays at the level of intent, no tooling, no fixture mechanics, no concrete scenario. |
| **PWA TSD §13, Testing Strategy** (the org's actual operative reference, cited by every other TSD including ours) | Names the real tools (Vitest, Storybook `play`, Playwright), states a real philosophy ("the cheapest layer that proves a behaviour wins, no duplicated coverage"), names *specific real business logic* to test ("Contentful → component data mapping, locale/currency transforms, Global-e pricing/tax branching..."), describes the actual Gherkin-first team workflow, and, most relevant to the Jesse conversation, **explicitly documents the fixture mechanism**: *"E2E specs are parameterised by `SITE_ID` from day one... site-specific baseUrl, currency, checkout owner, tax model, and consent default supplied by a fixture rather than hardcoded."* |

## What this actually tells us about specificity

The template alone sets a low bar, table-shaped, mapped to success criteria, that's genuinely achievable at spike/design stage without inventing detail. But the org's own real precedent (PWA TSD) goes considerably further, naming actual tools, actual fixture mechanics, actual selector conventions, not because the template demanded it, but because that document is the standing architecture reference every other TSD leans on rather than repeating.

That reframes the honest answer: our §6 is defensibly lean *for a spike*, per the template's minimum and per our own "tests belong to downstream stories" framing. But the PWA TSD already has the answer to the exact gap Jesse's asking about, a fixture-based, parameterised pattern (there for `SITE_ID`/region, not yet for Contentful content). Nobody has written the Contentful-specific version of that same pattern down anywhere, not in our TSD, not in the PWA TSD, not in Jesse's own conventions page, not in the three new backlog tickets we found. So the real gap isn't "our TSD isn't specific enough", it's that **the org has an established precedent for exactly this kind of problem, and it just hasn't been extended to cover Contentful yet.** That's a strong, concrete point to bring into the Jesse call: propose extending the PWA TSD's own `SITE_ID`-fixture pattern to Contentful test content, rather than presenting it as a brand new idea.

```
Hey Jesse, quick context ahead of our discussion.

What this spike is about:
SFCC-249 is a TSD for how Contentful-authored editorial content (banners, promo blocks, etc.) gets shown on the right SFCC page and not on others. Example: a banner that should only appear on the "Dresses" category page. The design (proposed, not built yet) works by tagging a Contentful entry with an SFCC category or product ID, then having the server filter which entries render for a given page.

Current state:
Design only right now. The actual content fetch is still client-side today, the server-side filtering this design relies on isn't built yet.

What we need to test, from a QA angle:
- The right content shows on the scoped page, and doesn't show anywhere else.
- Since the content is CMS-managed (editors can change it anytime), we can't test against "whatever's really live." We need known, dedicated test content, the same way product tests already use fixed SKUs (E2E_STANDARD_PRODUCT_SKU, etc.).
- The PWA TSD already has a similar fixture pattern for regional testing (tests parameterised by SITE_ID, with region-specific fixtures instead of hardcoded values). We think the same idea extends naturally to Contentful test content, just needs deciding together.

What's still blocking concrete test cases:
Three things aren't resolved yet, so this discussion is about agreeing an approach, not writing test cases today:
1. The actual server-side filtering mechanism isn't built.
2. Whether inserting Contentful content into a product grid breaks pagination, open question.
3. How a product page mixes Contentful content and SFCC content in one accordion, undecided.

One more thing worth flagging:
A few new backlog tickets (SFCC-304/305/306) currently assume E2E testing will wait for real, Zimmermann-authored content rather than using dedicated test fixtures, that's the opposite of the fixture approach above, worth reconciling.

Link to the TSD: https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/346783750

Thanks!
```
